Wing color here is inherited, not dyed; the share of dark moths changed over generations.
The data show a change in the forest population, not migration.
Light moths were eaten more on dark bark; lichen loss did not stop their breeding.

why.correct: Start at 90 (1950): <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>90</mn></mrow><mn>90</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>≈</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>78</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{20 - 90}{90} \times 100 \approx -78\%</annotation></semantics></math>. The share of dark moths fell by about 78% as the bark grew light again.
The same process ran in reverse once the environment changed back.
options: Laws changed the bark; moth color changed in the population through survival and breeding.
Right: as soot fell and lichen returned, dark moths fell from 85% to 20%.
Dark moths were still 20% of the catch in 2000.
The share of dark moths fell from 85% to 20% after 1970.

why.correct: Adaptations are heritable and helpful in the environment where the organism lives.
options: Changes within one life are not passed on, so they are not adaptations in this sense.
An adaptation is a trait that helps in the organism’s environment.
Right: it is inherited and it raises survival or reproduction.
Learned behaviors are not passed on in genes, so they are not adaptations in this sense.

why.correct: Look for a heritable trait changing in frequency across generations.
options: A change in one individual within its lifetime is not natural selection.
A stable population size says nothing about which traits are favored.
Learning is not passed on in genes.
Right: a change in the share of a heritable trait over generations is the result of selection.

why.correct: Variation first, then selection, then inheritance.
When change is fast relative to generation time, a population may not adapt in time.
options: Right: a slowly reproducing species has few generations for selection to act before conditions pass its limits.
Selection works on any population with heritable variation, moving or not.
Heritable traits are passed on; the problem is the speed of change.
Warmer water stresses corals; it does not speed up their reproduction.

why.correct: Variation, inheritance, and different survival or reproduction: those make selection work.
options: Right: without variation there is nothing to select.
Right: only heritable traits shift from one generation to the next.
Individuals do not change their inherited traits on demand; selection works on existing variation.
Selection happens everywhere, not only on islands.

why.correct: Explain an adaptation by how it raised survival or reproduction over generations.
options: Foxes do not choose their inherited coat color.
Right: the trait raised survival and reproduction, so it became common over generations.
The color is inherited; cold does not bleach it.
Foxes elsewhere have red, gray or brown fur.

why.correct: Low genetic diversity limits a population’s ability to adapt.
options: If the frogs are similar, they are also likely to share any weakness.
Their genetic variety differs, and that changes how they respond.
Right: genetic variety is the raw material natural selection works on.
Populations with resistant individuals can adapt to a disease over generations.

why.correct: Give the direction and the start and end values.
options: Right: biomass rises at every step, most of all as trees take over.
Biomass is higher at 150 years (30.0) than at 60 (18.0).
It reaches 30.0 kg per m² by 150 years.
Larger plants add biomass; the total rises.

why.correct: Start at 12 species: <math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mn>38</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>12</mn></mrow><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{38 - 12}{12} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="env-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">≈</mo><mn>216.7</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\approx 216.7\%</annotation></semantics></math>.
The key question is whether soil was present at the start.
options: Primary succession needs no soil; these fields had soil.
Right: an abandoned field keeps its soil and seeds, so succession is secondary.
Pioneer species appear in both kinds; the starting soil decides the kind.
Bare rock would make it primary, and these fields had soil.

why.correct: Richness often peaks in the middle stages, when early and late species overlap.
options: Biomass keeps rising, so the soil still supports more plant growth.
Oaks and hickories are most common at 150 years.
Right: in a mature forest a few large trees dominate and shade out some plants that need light.
They do not here: biomass rises while richness dips.

why.correct: The passage compares the two areas and states which recovered faster.
options: Plants sprouted the first summer where soil, roots and seeds survived.
Gophers dug soil after the eruption; they did not cause it.
The passage says the Pumice Plain recovered slowly.
Right: plants sprouted the first summer where soil remained, but slowly on the Pumice Plain.

why.correct: Primary succession starts with no soil and no surviving organisms.
options: Right: no soil and no surviving life is the starting point of primary succession.
The direction does not decide the kind of succession.
The size does not decide the kind of succession.
A name does not show anything about soil.

why.correct: Anything that brings back soil, seeds or nutrients makes succession faster.
options: The gophers brought soil up, not down.
Right: mixing old soil into the ash gives plants nutrients, water storage and buried seeds.
Fresh ash lacks the nutrients and organisms of old soil.
Gophers eat some plants, but bringing soil up helps more plants grow.

why.correct: Primary succession starts on surfaces with no soil.
options: Soil remains after a fire, so that is secondary succession.
An old field keeps its soil, so that is secondary succession.
Right: the glacier scraped the land to bare rock with no soil.
Floods leave soil, often adding more, so that is secondary.

why.correct: Pioneer species change the site so that later species can live there.
options: Lichens are tiny and do not block other species; they make room for them.
Lichens do not eat seeds; they make their food by photosynthesis.
Trees need soil, which takes a long time to form.
Right: lichens release acids that weather rock, and their remains add organic matter, the start of soil.

why.correct: Rock, then pioneers that start soil, then plants that need soil, then shrubs and trees, then a mature community.
Succession builds soil and biomass, replaces pioneers with longer-lived species, and makes the community more stable. Only the soil statement is correct.
options: Trees are larger and longer-lived than grasses, so total biomass increases.
Right: plants and decomposers add organic matter to the soil.
Pioneers are replaced by later species as conditions change.
Mature communities are usually more stable.

why.correct: Secondary succession follows any disruption that leaves soil.
options: Right: soil remains, so it is secondary, and sun-loving pioneers grow first in the gaps.
There is no bare rock; the soil is still there.
The disruption resets the community, so succession begins again.
What decides primary or secondary is the soil, not the trees.

why.correct: Name what secondary succession starts with, what primary succession must do first, and the result.
The slow step is building soil; supplying soil and seeds speeds succession.
options: Pioneers will come, but poor soil makes the early stages slow.
Right: adding soil and seeds skips the slow early stages.
Oaks are late-stage plants; they do not make a meadow and grow poorly in bare, packed ground.
Gravel blocks soil formation and makes plant growth harder.

why.correct: Any gradual replacement of one community by another in stages is succession.
options: Filling over centuries is a slow change, not a yearly event.
The pond is changing into a different community; that is succession.
Right: the community changes in a series of stages as the site itself changes.
The species present change, not the traits of one species.
